title: Keep awake (Mark 13:28–37)
hookLine: learn from the fig tree; no one knows the hour; watch

lines: LEARN A PARABLE OF THE FIG TREE.
cards: Bare sticks on Monday, a green haze by Friday. Nobody needs a calendar to read a tree in spring. Jesus uses that picture, and it's a fig tree again.

In the King James Bible: "Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near." A few days ago a fig tree in leaf meant disappointment.
Now tender leaves are a sign of something coming. After a whole chapter of strange and frightening images, he ends with a tree, a doorkeeper, and one word.

teach.h: NOT EVEN THE SON KNOWS THE HOUR.
teach.b: First, a sentence that stops readers short: "But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father." Not even the Son.
Whatever else it means, it leaves no room for anyone to set a date. So what do you do if you can't know when? He tells a tiny story.
A man goes on a journey, gives each servant their own work, and tells the doorkeeper to watch.

You don't know when the master comes: evening, midnight, cockcrow, or morning, the four watches of the night. Some readers notice that Mark's next chapters pass through each of them. An evening supper.
A garden at night where friends fall asleep. A rooster crowing. A morning trial.
Then the speech's final word: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch."
In Greek, grēgoreite, keep awake, stay alert. Watching isn't staring at the sky. The servants are busy with their own work.
It's doing today's work awake. Now look back. This week: Caesar's coin, whose wife, the greatest commandment, a widow's mite, not one stone, the days of distress, and keep awake.
And the whole road: back on day two hundred it turned south with a question about marriage. Children in his arms. A rich man walking away.
Bartimaeus, a borrowed colt, the temple, a rejected stone.
Now the road has reached Jerusalem.

teach.h: WHAT I SAY UNTO YOU I SAY UNTO ALL, WATCH.

how: Some churches read this passage on the first Sunday of Advent, the season of watchful waiting before Christmas, and some Christians keep vigils or pray at fixed hours as a way of keeping awake.

o: stay alert, doing today's work while you wait
keep your eyes on the sky, looking for signs
work out the date when the end will come

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus gave a date for the end
"of that day and that hour knoweth no man" — not even the Son.
in the story, each servant is given work to do
the master gives "to every man his work", and the doorkeeper watches.
watching means staring at the sky
the servants each have their own work; watching is doing it awake.

games.q: you're the doorkeeper. the master has left, and you don't know if he's coming at evening, midnight, cockcrow or morning. what do you do?
o: sleep now and wake at dawn.
games.why: watch. "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." and some readers find those same four watches in Mark's next chapters.

practice: With your eyes open if you like, notice five things around you that you've stopped seeing: the light on the wall, the sound of the fridge, the weight of your body in the chair.
Then ask what today's work actually is, not next month's; the doorkeeper guards just the door, tonight. If you pray, you can ask to be awake to what God is doing right now.

wordCard.voice: Keep awake. No one knows the hour, not even the Son, so the servants do today's work, watchful.

orig.note: Greek: keep awake, watch. the last word of the speech, Mark 13:37.

carryVoice: Your line: watch. One word, for everyone who hears it. That's a whole week done.
